DISCUSSION
A functioning PLC controlled system that is well designed, is efficient and cost-effective.

Problems may arise, however, and an organized approach to troubleshooting helps identify and correct most problems quickly.
The first step to troubleshooting a PLC controlled system is to observe the operation of the system.
Make notes about the problems observed and identify the areas functioning correctly. Try to logically identify possible causes.
Using the programming device to watch the input and output information as displayed in the programming software can help locate the problem area.
Use any built-in test features available to verify the operation of certain elements in order to eliminate them as possible causes.
Troubleshooting flowcharts or guides are often available and are helpful for identifying the cause, or at least reducing the list of possible causes.
2. Use The Programming Device 4. Consult Flow Charts

A PLC controlled system can be divided into 5 possible problem areas from the most likely to fail to least likely to fail. C System Problem Areas Elements of the System Wiring between Elements and I/O Modules I/O Modules PLC Processor Hardware

The elements of the system include the mechanical switches, motors, and sensors. These are some of the most likely causes of a problem since they are subjected to wear and possible eventual failure.... Modules I/O Modules PLC Processor Hardware

The wiring between the elements and the I/O terminals is also a very likely place for failure since faulty wiring or mechanical problems can interrupt or short the signals. fail. ween Elements and I/O Modules I/O Modules PLC Processor Hardware

The I/O modules usually contain built-in protection factors but these may be damaged if subjected to voltages or loads which exceed specifications. subject to wear out and fail. ween Elements and I/O Modules I/O Modules PLC Processor Hardware
Observing the I/O status lights may help determine if the I/O module is functioning properly.

The PLC processor hardware is not likely to fail since modern microcomputer hardware is quite reliable when operating within manufacturer's specifications. to wear out and fail. ween Elements and I/O Modules I/O Modules PLC Processor Hardware
The system usually shuts down completely if the PLC hardware fails, but minor faults may be identified using the processor module's status lights.

The ladder logic program is least likely to be the cause of the problem if the program was operating properly at one time. manufacturer's specifications. to wear out and fail. ween Elements and I/O Modules I/O Modules PLC Processor Hardware
The leading reason a program causes problems is if an unanticipated condition arises which the program was not designed to manage.anage.
Modifying the program to accept and handle the new condition should correct the problem.
If all other possible causes have been eliminated, however, then reloading the ladder logic program from the master copy is advisable.

The temperature of the liquid in a tank is represented by the air temperature around a heating element.
The liquid's level is manually controlled. The heater should not operate when the level is too low.
The potentiometer near TP6 is the thermostat used to set the desired temperature of the tank's liquid where 1 V = 10
The PLC compares the thermostat's value to the liquid's actual temperature and turns the heating element on or off as needed.
The PLC also illuminates the LED which corresponds to the liquid's temperature.
The over temperature sensor sets the maximum safe temperature level. The PLC illuminates a warning LED when the liquid's temperature exceeds this setting.
An error LED illuminates and the alarm sounds if the liquid's temperature exceeds the maximum safe level for more than
Pressing the lamp test button sounds the alarm, turns on the heater bulb, and illuminates all the LED's except the level indicator and overtemp LED's.
